answer_status_legend.OPEN: No defensible answer exists in this repository or in what could be verified this session. Decisions gated by it are not reasonable yet.
answer_status_legend.PARTIAL: We know the shape of the answer, or one official source establishes part of it; the remainder needs retrieval, money or a decision.
answer_status_legend.ANSWERED: Answered from official sources this session; the cited document is the answer.

questions.decision: Whether to spend money on a market-price feed at all (it gates R-02 and every strategy result).
questions.question: Which price source, at what granularity, and are we willing to pay for it?
questions.have: The Odds API's own documentation lists the NFL endpoint, the regions (us, us2, uk, eu, au), the markets (h2h, spreads, totals, quarter/half, player props from US and AU books only), per-bookmaker last_update timestamps, a free key tier, and historical odds from mid-2020 for the featured markets.
questions.missing: Actual licence terms, rate limits, whether prop and alternate-line history is deep enough to backtest, and whether their close-time snapshot definition matches the line we would actually get.
questions.how: Buy the cheapest tier for 3 weeks during the live season; log every response; compare our captured close to the line we could actually still take. Then decide.
questions.cost: Low: a trial plan plus one week of engineering; the real cost is the archival tier if it must be bought year by year.
questions.blocks: R-02, R-09, R-12, all strategy results

questions.decision: Whether 'beating the market' or 'beating our own model' is the objective.
questions.question: Is the goal to originate a line for its own sake (market-making) or to find mispriced bets (taking the market's line)?
questions.have: Both are stated in the brief; the site currently implements the second as a scored exercise and the first as a specification, because a proprietary number is only testable against realised outcomes and prices.
questions.missing: The owner's objective, and therefore which error metric is the target: Brier/calibration for a line generator, or closing-line value for a bet selector.
questions.how: One decision from the owner, written down before any model is tuned; the metric must be fixed in advance or the later numbers are not interpretable.
questions.cost: Free; it is a decision, not a purchase.

questions.decision: How much historical data is needed before any strategy can be believed.
questions.question: What is the minimum number of resolved bets per strategy, and over how many seasons, for a plausible edge to be separable from variance?
questions.have: The arithmetic is published on the gates page (normal approximation, two-sided 5%, 80% power, variance at the -110 break-even probability): a true 1% edge needs about 19,600 bets, 2% about 4,900, 3% about 2,200, 5% about 780. One NFL regular season offers 272 games, so a once-per-game strategy needs 8-18 seasons for a 1-3% edge, which is why the catalogue either needs many independent bets per game or must accept wide intervals.
questions.missing: Our own realised bet count, which is zero, and the correlation adjustment that inflates these numbers (a season-block bootstrap is the honest interval, not the normal approximation).
questions.how: Fix the target edge in advance, then let the required-n table, not the observed win rate, decide when to stop looking.
questions.cost: Free to decide; expensive to reach if the edge is small.

questions.decision: Whether the market's realised hold makes small edges unrecoverable in the bet types we care about.
questions.question: What hold do operators actually realise on NFL sides, totals and parlays, by state and season?
questions.have: Colorado's Division of Gaming published September 2026 handle of $546,819,852.87 with $4,743,419.32 in state tax, and August 2026 handle of $388,148,758.21 with $3,154,842.89 in tax; New Jersey reported $61,445,421 of sports wagering revenue for August 2026 (online $59,749,699, lounge $1,695,722), -25.0% year over year. The monthly operator-level PDFs that contain revenue against handle exist back through 2023 with revisions.
questions.missing: The bet-type breakdown (side vs total vs parlay) and a multi-month series we can use as a cost model. State tax is not the operator's gross win, so hold cannot be read off the tax number.
questions.how: Parse the Colorado monthly proceeds PDFs and the New Jersey completed-events tables for 24 months and compute realised hold distributions by month.
questions.cost: Free; a day of work to build the parser.

questions.decision: Whether parlays/SGPs are a place to hunt for edge or where the vig lives.
questions.question: Do operators win materially more on parlays than on singles in NFL, and does that gap survive a same-game-parlay discount?
questions.have: New Jersey's August 2026 release explains its revenue drop with a 'lower overall win percentage', and the trade press reporting that release attributes most of the year-over-year decline to parlay win percentage falling to 14.6% from 19.0%; the official PDF's completed-events table containing that split was not retrievable this session.
questions.missing: The official parlay-level handle/win table, and the same for NFL-specific months (September-January).
questions.how: Retrieve the later pages of the New Jersey monthly PDFs and any state that reports win by bet type; do not accept the secondary number as a fact.
questions.cost: Free; retrieval only.

questions.decision: Which operators can be used at all, and therefore which markets we can price against.
questions.question: In the owner's jurisdiction, which sportsbooks are licensed for NFL wagering, at what minimum age, and with what account and tax treatment?
questions.have: Nothing verified this session. State regulators publish the reports used above, which implies licensed operators in those states; Colorado's own page publishes the responsible-gambling resources.
questions.missing: The owner's jurisdiction and eligibility, the licensed-operator list there, and the tax treatment of winnings.
questions.how: Owner answers the jurisdiction question; then read that state's regulator page (or the national regulator outside the US) rather than a comparison site.
questions.cost: Free; requires the owner, so it is escalated not answered.

questions.decision: Whether a constructed parlay will actually stand.
questions.question: Which leg combinations does each target operator void, reprice, or refuse as correlated?
questions.have: One published operator house-rule document states that outside a Same Game Parlay or Progressive Parlay, a parlay containing two or more correlated selections may be void, that a non-SGP parlay 'shall never include two or more offers where the outcomes of which might turn out to be related', and that a void or push leg in a pre-live SGP triggers a reprice (all-void/push voids the ticket).
questions.missing: That document is snippet-verified from a licensed casino's copy of the operator's rules, not retrieved by us, and it is not the operator the owner would use. Rules for correlated SGP legs, and whether the SGP price is built with an explicit correlation adjustment, are per-operator and per-state.
questions.how: Read the live rulebook of each operator we would actually use and store it with a hash and a date, exactly as this repo already does for schedule sources.
questions.cost: Free; a few hours to build the rule-snapshot step.

questions.decision: What 'injury impact' means numerically, and whether we can measure it.
questions.question: Does the availability change we detect actually move the outcome distribution, or does the market already know?
questions.have: The official reporting vocabulary and its asymmetry: practice statuses are defined (Did Not Participate / Limited / Full), game statuses are Out, Doubtful, Questionable, a certain-to-play player is deliberately omitted from the Game Status Report, and deactivating an omitted player requires an explanation to the league. Week 10, 2026 shows this in practice: the 49ers listed six DNPs on the fetched page and no game-status designations at all, which is a legitimate state, not missing data.
questions.missing: A causal impact estimate per position and replacement tier. Without historical prices aligned to historical reports, any number we would publish is invented.
questions.how: Build the report-price-event dataset first (Q-01), then estimate impact on the deviation from the close, not on the win.
questions.cost: Data cost dominates; the modelling is standard.

questions.decision: Whether the roster rules the availability model encodes are current.
questions.question: Are the IR four-game minimum, eight return designations, 16-man practice squad and PUP/NFI activation windows still the 2026 rules?
questions.have: An official NFL article stating those rules, written around the 2022 offseason, plus the 2022 amendment report; the article's own dates and examples are 2022.
questions.missing: The current-year roster rules text or a 2026 official statement. Rules change by offseason agreement, and a stale rule silently corrupts every availability window we compute.
questions.how: Re-derive from the current league roster rules and each club's published transactions for a week; store the document, not a memory.
questions.cost: Free.

questions.decision: How depth charts are collected for all 32 clubs.
questions.question: Is there one official league-wide depth-chart source, or only 32 club pages with inconsistent cadence?
questions.have: The club page is real and dated ('Updated as of 11/10/26' for San Francisco), with per-position first/second/third strings and positions carrying only one or two names. The league's team-section depth-chart path returned a 404 page when tested this session, and the team transactions path also 404s at the URL we tried.
questions.missing: A reliable machine-readable availability for all 32 clubs, the true update cadence per club, and whether a club can quietly leave a stale chart up (which would look like a roster improvement).
questions.how: Probe all 32 club sites, record HTTP status and the 'Updated as of' date per club, and treat any chart older than the club's median cadence as stale and unusable for that week.
questions.cost: Free; a maintenance tax forever, because club sites change.

questions.decision: Whether snap-count-driven prop signals are possible on a schedule that fits betting.
questions.question: Can we get participation data before the decision cut-off, given the league publishes tracking data the next day?
questions.have: The league's own documentation: Next Gen Stats is available the day after the game; box score and play-by-play update live during the game. Preseason film and data are excluded from that product.
questions.missing: A pre-kickoff source for projected or depth-derived usage that we trust, and a decision on whether to use a commercial projection vendor (which imports someone else's model into ours).
questions.how: Decide the cut-off (for example Friday 5 PM ET for props) and enumerate only fields available at that timestamp; that set is small and mostly derived from the injury report and the depth chart, which is a modelling constraint, not a data gap.
questions.cost: Free.

questions.decision: How a bet is settled, and whether we are allowed to settle it ourselves.
questions.question: What is the authoritative result source for a prop or a ticket, given that props settle on the league's official statistics?
questions.have: The repo already ingests official league game data and box-score-level results; the regulator rule we found says an operator may only accept a wager where the outcome can be verified and generated by a reliable and independent process, and the regulator may disapprove a data source.
questions.missing: The official league stats definition for each prop we would price (for example how a quarterback sack or a half-point in a rush-yards prop is decided), and the operator's own settlement wording.
questions.how: Take the statistic definition from the league's official stat standard document and the settlement from the operator's rulebook, and store both per season; a mid-season definition change must be visible in the ledger.
questions.cost: Free; requires discipline.

questions.decision: Whether 'our line' can be used for anything other than internal comparison.
questions.question: What are the legal and integrity constraints on publishing or betting against our own prices, including official-league-data requirements?
questions.have: An Indiana rule (2020 emergency text) on wager and data-source requirements, and the general fact that state regimes decide whether operators must use official league data; the repo documents no legal advice anywhere.
questions.missing: A jurisdiction-specific answer, ideally from the regulator's current codified text, and whether the owner's use (private modelling) even engages it. This is a legal question, not a data question.
questions.cost: Potentially a one-hour consultation; nothing here should substitute for it.
questions.how: Escalate to counsel with the concrete plan (states, operators, whether anything is offered to third parties).

questions.decision: Where the boundary between verified and convenient data sits.
questions.question: Do we allow aggregator injury detail (injury type, 'rest', reporter attribution) in the store, and if so, in which columns?
questions.have: Aggregators publish more than the official report does, for example listing Mike Evans with an Achilles issue and Trent Williams as a non-injury rest, where the official page shows only a practice status. Our own registry keeps them as cross-check only.
questions.missing: A rule for how to store such fields without laundering them into verified facts: separate columns, separate table, or not at all.
questions.how: Adopt the strict rule already used in this repo: an unconfirmable value is blank and flagged; keep secondary detail in a clearly labelled secondary table that gates cannot read.
questions.cost: Free; it is a discipline decision.

questions.decision: What the leaderboard rewards are, and who may enter.
questions.question: Are rewards cash, credits, compute or recognition; is entry open to third parties; and does the reward structure create a rule-breaking incentive?
questions.have: A complete scoring and governance design on the leaderboard page: gate-pass promotion, CLV-based ranking, minimum-sample floors, tamper-evident submission ledger, tie-breaks, and a prohibition on stake-pool participation prizes.
questions.missing: The owner's budget and form of reward, plus a check that a prize competition is permissible where the owner operates (prize competitions have their own rules, separate from gambling law).
questions.how: Owner picks one of the three reward models proposed; then freeze the rules for a full season before entries open, since post-hoc scoring changes destroy the comparison.
questions.cost: Whatever the owner decides; the paper-trading variant costs nothing.

questions.decision: What a strategy must be worth before it gets funded.
questions.question: What is the promotion bar: gate pass only, or gate pass plus a minimum banked edge, plus a live-paper trial?
questions.have: Gate thresholds are written (G-01..G-18) with the intent that no single metric promotes a strategy: significance, CLV, calibration, cost sensitivity and stability must all pass simultaneously, and multiple-comparison control (Benjamini-Hochberg across the catalogue) is mandatory because a 14-strategy catalogue manufactures winners at 5% significance.
questions.missing: The owner's funding policy per strategy (unit size, exposure cap, kill switch) and whether the first season is paper-only.
questions.how: Decide unit sizing and caps in writing before the first bet; a size decided after the results are seen is not a policy.
questions.cost: Free to decide; the exposure is the cost.

questions.decision: How much of the site's existing free-time work is in scope for the NFL section.
questions.question: Does the NFL section reuse the radio/schedule dashboard's data and verification gate, or run a parallel stack?
questions.have: This section reuses the repo's official snapshot for schedule context and copies its verification conventions (per-row source links, allowlisted official hosts, blank-plus-flag) while keeping its own builder, verifier and CI job so that no file owned by the other workstreams is touched.
questions.missing: A decision on whether to merge the two navigations and gates into one site (SG-02 proposes the options).
questions.how: Owner chooses: keep separate, share navigation only, or fully integrate with one verifier. The integration path is a follow-up task with a defined file scope.
questions.cost: Low; the risk is merge conflict with the four open PRs.

questions.decision: What 'no manual input' means at the data boundary.
questions.question: Which required inputs can be obtained without a human, and which cannot?
questions.have: What was done with no manual input in this session: official pages retrieved and quoted, a repository-wide verification gate built and run, all pages generated from data, PR and Pages publication. What cannot be done without the owner: buying a feed, opening an account, choosing a jurisdiction, choosing a bankroll, or deciding between proposed options.
questions.missing: Nothing - the boundary is defined; it just means the final decisions stay with the owner by design.
questions.how: Keep the rule: agents build and verify, the owner decides money, law and priority; the suggestions page is the interface for that.
questions.cost: Free.

questions.decision: How the site stays honest as it grows.
questions.question: Who is accountable when a published row goes stale or a source changes underneath the table?
questions.have: The repo already publishes a snapshot-age disclosure on every page of the radio dashboard, and this section stamps each page with a build time plus its own source retrieval date; the verifier fails a row whose official claim has no fetched official source.
questions.missing: A refresh schedule (the collector workflow exists but is not yet wired to a cron with alerts) and a definition of staleness per table type, for example depth charts older than the club's own cadence, or injury data older than the last official report day.
questions.how: Wire the dispatch workflow to a schedule, add a staleness threshold per dataset, and publish a stale badge rather than deleting the row.
questions.cost: Free; uses the existing Actions capacity.

questions.decision: Which correlation values are allowed to enter a price at all.
questions.question: Do we price parlays with our own measured correlations, with published bounds, or refuse to price tickets we cannot measure?
questions.have: The method: pairwise outcome correlation estimated from our own resolved history; until measured, the ticket is priced at the bound implied by its marginals and flagged 'correlation unverified'; the fact that operators reprice or void correlated combos (Q-07) means a wrong correlation does not just misprice it, it can invalidate the ticket.
questions.missing: Any measured value: we have zero resolved tickets, so the correlation column is blank by rule, not zero.
questions.how: Run the first full season with tickets logged but unfunded; measure after; only then allow a correlated SGP into the funded set.
questions.cost: Free; costs a season of patience.

questions.decision: Whether 'remove luck' is achievable as stated or must be restated.
questions.question: What can we honestly promise about separating skill from variance in an NFL sample?
questions.have: The quantitative reality, published on the gates page: outcome variance per bet is bounded by the payoff structure, so the only levers are sample size, edge size and shrinkage toward zero. At -110 prices with a 55% true hit rate, the standard error of ROI is about 5.5 percentage points at 300 bets, so a 95% interval spans roughly +-10.8 points - a coin-flip record can look like a 5-10% winner for a whole season. That is why the leaderboard ranks luck-adjusted value (entry price versus close), not records.
questions.missing: The owner's acceptance of that framing: if a strategy's promise is 'it won last month', no gate in this catalogue will ever validate it.
questions.how: Agree the metric before the competition starts, in writing, and treat any later metric change as a new competition.
questions.cost: Free; this is the decision that most protects the money.

questions.decision: What the 2026 season can and cannot be used for.
questions.question: Is the currently captured season data sufficient to start live paper trading this month?
questions.have: The 2026 schedule and event rows from the repository snapshot (2026-11-02), the Week 10 official injury report pages fetched today, and the 49ers depth chart dated 11/10/26; the league's published important dates for the season structure are in the snapshot manifest.
questions.missing: Prices (all of them), and the snapshot is 11 days old, so any transaction, roster move or time change after 2026-11-02 is invisible here. Kickoff times for some rows are still TBD in the snapshot.
questions.how: Run the collector, then start a paper season for the remaining weeks with a strict pre-kickoff cut-off, accepting that a partial season cannot pass the sample-size gates - its value is calibration practice, not promotion.
questions.cost: Low.
